questions.stem: An order service calls an inventory service synchronously over HTTP. During sales events the inventory service slows down, and orders fail with timeouts. The orders do not need to be processed instantly. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Increase the HTTP client timeout in the order service
options.rationale: Longer waits keep the services tightly coupled and still fail when the backlog grows.

options.text: Add Amazon Route 53 weighted routing in front of the inventory service
options.rationale: Weighted DNS splits traffic between endpoints but does not buffer requests.

options.text: Run both services on one larger Amazon EC2 instance so that calls between them stay local
options.rationale: Co-locating the services keeps the synchronous dependency and adds a single point of failure.

options.text: Send each order to an Amazon SQS queue and let the inventory service poll the queue
options.rationale: The queue absorbs bursts and decouples the two services, so the inventory service works at its own pace.

questions.explanation: The clues are a slow downstream service and orders that can wait, so put a queue between the services. A longer timeout is the tempting fix, but it keeps the call synchronous and still fails as the backlog grows.

questions.stem: A REST API in Amazon API Gateway starts a report that takes several minutes to build. Clients currently wait on the request and receive timeout errors. What should the developer do?

options.text: Return a job ID, queue the work in Amazon SQS, and let the client fetch the report later
options.rationale: The API responds immediately and a worker builds the report asynchronously.

options.text: Invoke the report function synchronously and raise the HTTP timeout on the client and the API
options.rationale: Holding a request open for minutes is fragile, and API Gateway's integration timeout is short by default.

options.text: Enable API Gateway caching for the report resource
options.rationale: Caching reuses earlier responses; it does not make the first build faster.

options.text: Build the report inside an API Gateway mapping template
options.rationale: Mapping templates transform payloads; they cannot run long jobs.

questions.explanation: Long-running work belongs behind an asynchronous pattern: accept the request, queue it, and let the client poll or be notified.

questions.stem: An application that writes to Amazon DynamoDB sometimes receives throttling errors during traffic spikes. How should the application handle these errors?

options.text: Retry the request immediately in a loop until it succeeds
options.rationale: Immediate retries add load at the moment the table is already throttling.

options.text: Retry the request with exponential backoff and jitter
options.rationale: Spacing out retries with random delays gives capacity time to recover and avoids synchronized retry storms.

options.text: Discard the request and log the error
options.rationale: Throttling errors are retryable, so dropping the write loses data unnecessarily.

options.text: Send the request to a table in another AWS Region
options.rationale: Switching Regions does not address throttling and leaves the data split across tables.

questions.explanation: Throttling errors are temporary, so retry them, but spread the retries out with exponential backoff and jitter, as the AWS SDKs do by default. Immediate retries are the trap: they add load while the table is already throttling.

questions.stem: A developer wants Amazon API Gateway to reject POST requests whose JSON body is missing required fields, before the backend is invoked. Which combination of steps will meet this requirement? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Add a Lambda authorizer that checks the body and denies requests with missing fields
options.rationale: Lambda authorizers decide whether a caller is allowed, and they do not receive the request body.

options.text: Create a model whose JSON schema marks the fields as required
options.rationale: The model describes the expected body as a JSON schema, including which fields are required.

options.text: Attach a usage plan and an API key to the method
options.rationale: Usage plans throttle and meter clients; they do not validate payloads.

options.text: Add a stage variable that lists the required fields
options.rationale: Stage variables are name-value settings for a stage, not validation rules.

options.text: Turn on a request validator for the method body that uses the model
options.rationale: API Gateway then checks the body against the model and returns 400 Bad Request when it does not match.

questions.explanation: The clue is rejecting bad bodies before the backend runs: a model defines the required fields and a request validator enforces it in API Gateway. A Lambda authorizer is the nearest distractor, but it decides who may call, not what the body contains.

questions.stem: A legacy backend expects request fields with different names than the ones that clients send to a REST API in Amazon API Gateway. The backend cannot be changed. What should the developer use?

options.text: A Lambda proxy integration that passes the request through to the backend unchanged
options.rationale: Proxy integrations forward the request as it is, so the field names would not change.

options.text: Cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) on the resource
options.rationale: CORS controls which browser origins may call the API.

options.text: A gateway response that rewrites error messages
options.rationale: Gateway responses customize errors from API Gateway itself, not normal requests.

options.text: A non-proxy integration with a mapping template that renames the fields
options.rationale: Mapping templates transform the request and response between the method and the integration.

questions.explanation: Use a non-proxy (custom) integration with mapping templates when the client and backend formats differ.

questions.stem: Sensors send readings to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. Readings from the same sensor must stay in order, and the load must spread across shards as more sensors are added. What should the producer use as the partition key?

options.text: The sensor ID
options.rationale: All records with the same partition key map to the same shard, and sequence numbers within a shard increase over time, so one sensor's readings stay in order.

options.text: A random value for each record
options.rationale: Random keys spread one sensor's readings across shards, so their order is not kept.

options.text: The current timestamp
options.rationale: Timestamps change with every record and spread one sensor across many shards.

options.text: The same constant value for every record
options.rationale: A single key sends all traffic to one shard and limits throughput.

questions.explanation: The partition key decides the shard, and sequence numbers order records within a shard, not across shards.

questions.stem: A company wants to load clickstream events into Amazon S3 in near real time, batched into files, without writing or running any consumer code. Which service meets this requirement?

options.text: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams with a custom consumer application
options.rationale: A custom consumer is code that must be written and run, which the requirement rules out.

options.text: Amazon Data Firehose
options.rationale: Firehose buffers incoming records and delivers them to destinations such as Amazon S3 with no consumer code.

options.text: Amazon SQS with an Amazon EC2 worker
options.rationale: A worker would have to be written and operated to move the messages to S3.

options.text: AWS Step Functions
options.rationale: Step Functions orchestrates workflows; it is not a streaming delivery service.

questions.explanation: Firehose is the managed way to stream data into storage and analytics destinations.

questions.stem: A Lambda function behind an API Gateway Lambda proxy integration reads event.body.orderId, but the value is always undefined even though clients send it. What is the cause?

options.text: The function's memory setting is too low to hold the whole request body
options.rationale: Memory size does not change how the body is delivered.

options.text: API Gateway removes request bodies unless caching is enabled
options.rationale: Caching has nothing to do with passing the body to the integration.

options.text: The body arrives as a JSON string that must be parsed first
options.rationale: In the proxy event, body is a string, so the code must deserialize it first.

options.text: The function needs a resource-based policy to read the body
options.rationale: Permissions control who can invoke the function, not what the event contains.

questions.explanation: Serialization matters at every boundary: parse incoming JSON strings, and return the response body as a string.

questions.stem: When an image is uploaded to an Amazon S3 bucket, two separate applications must each receive the event and process the image independently. Which solutions will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Send the event to one Amazon SQS standard queue that both applications poll
options.rationale: Each message is processed by only one consumer, so the applications would split the events.

options.text: Publish the event to an Amazon SNS topic with one Amazon SQS queue per application
options.rationale: SNS fans the event out so each queue gets its own copy.

options.text: Have the first application forward each event to the second after it finishes processing
options.rationale: This chains the applications, so a failure or delay in the first one stops the second.

options.text: Send the event to an Amazon SQS FIFO queue that both applications share
options.rationale: A FIFO queue still delivers each message to a single consumer.

options.text: Turn on Amazon EventBridge for the bucket, with a rule that targets both applications
options.rationale: EventBridge can route the same S3 event to several targets.

questions.explanation: Fan-out needs a copy per consumer: SNS-to-SQS or an EventBridge rule with several targets.

questions.stem: An application uses a foundation model in Amazon Bedrock to write product descriptions. The team expects to switch to a different model later and does not want to rewrite how requests and responses are formatted. What should the developer use?

options.text: The InvokeModel API with each model's native request body
options.rationale: InvokeModel uses model-specific payloads, so switching models means rewriting the request code.

options.text: A model hosted on Amazon EC2 behind an HTTP endpoint
options.rationale: Self-hosting adds infrastructure and does not give a common interface across models.

options.text: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to send prompts to the model
options.rationale: Kinesis streams data records; it is not a way to call a model.

options.text: The Amazon Bedrock Converse API
options.rationale: Converse gives a consistent request and response format across the models that support it.

questions.explanation: The clue is switching models without rewriting request code: Converse uses one message format across the models that support it. InvokeModel is the nearest distractor, but its request body is specific to each model.

questions.stem: Before writing any code for a new feature, a developer wants an AI tool to produce requirements, a technical design and a list of implementation tasks that can then be worked through. Which Kiro feature does this?

options.text: A spec
options.rationale: A Kiro spec produces requirements, design and tasks documents for a feature before implementation.

options.text: A steering file
options.rationale: Steering files give the agent standing guidance such as coding standards; they do not plan a feature.

options.text: An agent hook
options.rationale: Hooks run actions automatically on events such as saving a file.

options.text: An MCP server
options.rationale: MCP servers give the agent extra tools and data sources.

questions.explanation: Spec-driven development turns a feature request into requirements.md, design.md and tasks.md.

questions.stem: An order service publishes OrderPlaced and OrderCancelled events. New services that react to these events keep being added, and the team does not want to change the order service each time. What should the developer do?

options.text: Have the order service call each consuming service's HTTP endpoint directly after every order is placed
options.rationale: This couples the order service to every consumer; each new consumer needs a code change.

options.text: Send the events to one Amazon SQS queue that every consuming service polls
options.rationale: Each SQS message is processed by only one consumer, so the services would not each receive every event.

options.text: Write the events to a shared database table that each consuming service scans on a schedule
options.rationale: Polling a shared table couples services to one schema and adds delay and read cost.

options.text: Publish the events to an Amazon EventBridge event bus, with one rule per consuming service
options.rationale: Producers and consumers stay independent: a new consumer adds a rule without any change to the order service.

questions.explanation: An event bus with rules decouples producers from consumers: each consumer subscribes with its own event pattern.

questions.stem: An order workflow runs four Lambda functions in sequence. A failed step must be retried a few times, and if it still fails, a compensation function must undo the earlier steps. The developer wants this logic outside the function code. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: An AWS Step Functions state machine with Retry and Catch fields on its task states
options.rationale: Retry and Catch handle retries and route failures to a compensation state without custom code in the functions.

options.text: A first Lambda function that invokes the others synchronously and handles errors itself
options.rationale: That keeps the orchestration and error handling inside function code, and the first function pays for the whole wait.

options.text: An Amazon SNS topic that each function publishes to when it finishes
options.rationale: SNS fans out messages but has no notion of steps, retries per step or compensation.

options.text: An Amazon EventBridge scheduled rule that runs each function a few minutes apart
options.rationale: A schedule does not pass results between steps or react to failures.

questions.explanation: Step Functions orchestrates multi-step workflows and handles errors declaratively with Retry and Catch.

questions.stem: Transactions for the same bank account must be processed in the order they were sent, while transactions for different accounts are processed in parallel. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Set the queue's visibility timeout to 0 seconds
options.rationale: This makes messages visible again immediately and causes duplicate processing; it does nothing for order.

options.text: Set the message group ID to the account ID
options.rationale: Messages for one account stay in order, and different accounts form different groups that can be processed in parallel.

options.text: Use the same message group ID for every message
options.rationale: One group forces every transaction into a single ordered stream, so nothing runs in parallel.

options.text: Use an Amazon SQS FIFO queue
options.rationale: FIFO queues keep order within a message group.

options.text: Use an Amazon SQS standard queue with a delivery delay
options.rationale: Standard queues do not guarantee order, and a delay does not create one.

questions.explanation: In a FIFO queue, ordering is per message group, so the group ID decides what is ordered and what can run in parallel.

questions.stem: A script lists the objects in an Amazon S3 bucket by calling ListObjectsV2 once. The bucket has 25,000 objects, but the script processes only the first 1,000. How should the developer fix the script?

options.text: Set MaxKeys to 25000 so that every key comes back in a single response
options.rationale: MaxKeys can lower the page size but cannot raise it above 1,000 keys per response.

options.text: Follow the continuation token in each response, or use the SDK's paginator
options.rationale: Each response returns at most 1,000 keys; the continuation token or a paginator fetches the rest.

options.text: Switch to the older ListObjects API
options.rationale: It is paginated the same way and is not recommended for new code.

options.text: Retry the call with exponential backoff until every key is returned
options.rationale: Nothing failed; the response is one page of results, so retrying returns the same page.

questions.explanation: List APIs return results in pages. Code must follow the continuation token, or use an SDK paginator that does it for you.

questions.stem: A product page calls a recommendation service. When that service is slow or down, the whole page fails to load. The page must still load, even if it shows no recommendations. What should the developer do?

options.text: Retry the call to the recommendation service until it responds successfully
options.rationale: Waiting on a failing dependency makes the page slower and can add load to the struggling service.

options.text: Increase the page's timeout so that the recommendation call has more time to finish
options.rationale: A longer wait makes users wait longer and still fails when the service is down.

options.text: Use a short timeout, and show default or cached content if the call fails
options.rationale: This is graceful degradation: the page keeps working without the optional dependency.

options.text: Return an error page that asks the user to try again later
options.rationale: That is the current failure; the requirement is that the page still loads.

questions.explanation: A soft dependency should not take down the caller. Use timeouts and fall back to a reduced experience.

questions.stem: A worker processes payment messages from an Amazon SQS standard queue. Occasionally a customer is charged twice for one payment message. What should the developer do?

options.text: Increase the queue's message retention period so that duplicate messages expire sooner
options.rationale: Retention controls how long unprocessed messages are kept, not whether they are delivered more than once.

options.text: Delete each message before charging the customer
options.rationale: If processing then fails, the payment is lost.

options.text: Lower the number of messages received per call to 1
options.rationale: Batch size does not change at-least-once delivery.

options.text: Record each payment ID with a conditional write, and skip IDs that are already recorded
options.rationale: Standard queues deliver at least once, so the consumer must make a repeated message harmless.

questions.explanation: Design consumers of at-least-once delivery to be idempotent, for example with a DynamoDB conditional write on a unique ID.

questions.stem: A REST API in Amazon API Gateway uses a Lambda non-proxy (custom) integration. When the function throws a validation error, clients receive HTTP 200 with the error message in the body. Clients must receive HTTP 400 instead. What should the developer configure?

options.text: A 400 method response, and an integration response whose regex matches the error message
options.rationale: In a non-proxy integration, API Gateway maps Lambda errors to status codes by matching the error message.

options.text: Return an object whose statusCode field is 400 from the function, as proxy integrations expect
options.rationale: That shape is for proxy integrations; a non-proxy integration passes it through as a 200 body.

options.text: A request validator on the method
options.rationale: Request validators check incoming requests; they do not map backend errors to status codes.

options.text: A gateway response for the DEFAULT_4XX type
options.rationale: Gateway responses customize errors that API Gateway itself generates, not errors returned by the integration.

questions.explanation: With a custom Lambda integration, error mapping is done in the integration responses, keyed on the error message.

questions.stem: Five consumer applications read the same Amazon Kinesis data stream. They compete for each shard's read throughput, and their reads are getting throttled. Each application needs its own read throughput. What should the developer use?

options.text: A larger batch size in each GetRecords call
options.rationale: Bigger batches still share the shard's read limit.

options.text: Enhanced fan-out consumers
options.rationale: Each registered consumer gets its own dedicated read throughput per shard, pushed over HTTP/2.

options.text: One Amazon SQS queue per application, filled by the producer
options.rationale: This rebuilds fan-out by hand and loses Kinesis replay and ordering features.

options.text: A longer data retention period on the stream
options.rationale: Retention controls how long records are kept, not read throughput.

questions.explanation: Shared-throughput consumers split each shard's read capacity; enhanced fan-out gives every consumer its own.

questions.stem: Code that uses the low-level DynamoDB client reads items as nested objects such as {"S": "Alice"} and {"N": "42"}. The developer wants to work with plain strings and numbers instead. What should the developer do?

options.text: Store every attribute as a string so that values are returned unwrapped
options.rationale: This loses number and set types and does not change the response format of the low-level client.

options.text: Use a Scan instead of GetItem
options.rationale: Every low-level read returns the same typed format.

options.text: Use the SDK's document client or a type deserializer to convert values
options.rationale: These helpers serialize and deserialize attribute values so code works with ordinary objects.

options.text: Enable DynamoDB Streams with the NEW_IMAGE view
options.rationale: Streams also use the typed format and do not change how reads are returned.

questions.explanation: The low-level API uses typed attribute values; SDK document clients and deserializers convert them to native types.

questions.stem: A team uses Kiro. The agent keeps writing code that ignores the team's naming conventions and preferred libraries, so developers repeat the same instructions in every chat. How should the team give the agent this guidance once?

options.text: Paste the conventions at the start of every chat session
options.rationale: This is the repetition the team wants to avoid.

options.text: Create an agent hook that runs on every file save
options.rationale: Hooks automate actions on events; they are not the place to store standing guidance.

options.text: Write the conventions as comments at the top of every source file
options.rationale: Comments scattered through files are not a reliable or maintainable way to guide the agent.

options.text: Add steering files to the project that describe the conventions
options.rationale: Steering files give the agent persistent project knowledge, so it follows the conventions without repeated instructions.

questions.explanation: Kiro steering files hold persistent guidance such as conventions and preferred libraries.

questions.stem: A chat application calls a foundation model through Amazon Bedrock with the Converse API. Users wait several seconds and then see the whole answer at once. They want to see the text appear as it is generated. What should the developer do?

options.text: Call ConverseStream and render each text chunk as it arrives
options.rationale: ConverseStream returns the response as a stream of events, so the app can display partial text.

options.text: Lower the maximum number of tokens in the request
options.rationale: Shorter answers arrive sooner, but they are still returned all at once and may be cut off.

options.text: Call the Converse API asynchronously from a Lambda function
options.rationale: The response is still returned in one piece.

options.text: Cache the model's answers in Amazon ElastiCache and serve repeat questions from it
options.rationale: Caching helps only repeated questions and does not stream new answers.

questions.explanation: Use the streaming variant of the Bedrock API to show output as it is generated.

questions.stem: An Amazon EventBridge rule sends events to a Lambda function. Sometimes the function is unavailable, and some events are never processed. Events that cannot be delivered must be kept for later reprocessing. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Add a queue policy that lets EventBridge send messages to the dead-letter queue
options.rationale: EventBridge needs permission to send to the queue. The console adds it, but API and infrastructure-as-code setups must add it themselves.

options.text: Archive the event bus and replay every event each hour
options.rationale: Replaying everything reprocesses events that already succeeded.

options.text: Add a second rule with the same pattern that targets the same function
options.rationale: Both rules would fail in the same way, and successful events would be processed twice.

options.text: Configure an Amazon SQS dead-letter queue on the rule's target
options.rationale: Events that still cannot be delivered after retries are sent to the queue instead of being dropped.

options.text: Increase the Lambda function's timeout
options.rationale: A longer timeout does not help when the target is unavailable.

questions.explanation: Targets retry by default. An SQS dead-letter queue, with a queue policy that lets EventBridge send to it, keeps events that still cannot be delivered.

questions.stem: A chat application must push new messages from the backend to connected browsers as soon as they arrive, without the browsers polling. Which Amazon API Gateway API type should the developer use?

options.text: A REST API with caching turned on for the messages resource
options.rationale: Caching serves repeated requests faster, but clients still have to ask for new messages.

options.text: A WebSocket API
options.rationale: WebSocket APIs keep a two-way connection open, so the backend can send messages to clients at any time.

options.text: An HTTP API with a Lambda proxy integration on each route
options.rationale: HTTP APIs answer requests; the server cannot push messages without a request.

options.text: A private REST API reached through an interface VPC endpoint
options.rationale: Private APIs limit where calls come from; they still follow request and response.

questions.explanation: WebSocket APIs support server-to-client messages over a persistent connection.

questions.stem: An application must read a 20 GB object from Amazon S3 as fast as possible, using several worker threads at the same time. How should the code read the object?

options.text: Call GetObject once and wait for the whole body before processing
options.rationale: A single request downloads the object serially, which is the slow path.

options.text: Copy the object to an EBS volume first with an S3 Lifecycle rule
options.rationale: Lifecycle rules change storage classes or expire objects; they do not copy to EBS.

options.text: Fetch byte ranges of the object in parallel
options.rationale: Byte-range fetches let each worker download its own part of the object at the same time.

options.text: Turn on S3 Versioning so that several versions can be read in parallel
options.rationale: Versions are separate copies over time, not parts of one object to read in parallel.

questions.explanation: Parallel byte-range GETs give higher total throughput than one whole-object request, and smaller ranges make retries faster when a request is interrupted.

questions.stem: Clickstream events must be kept in order per user, read by three different applications, and replayable from the last 24 hours when an application has a bug. Which service fits these requirements?

options.text: An Amazon SQS standard queue
options.rationale: Ordering is best-effort, and each message is processed by one consumer and then deleted.

options.text: An Amazon SNS standard topic
options.rationale: SNS pushes each message once to subscribers and does not keep it for replay.

options.text: An Amazon SQS FIFO queue with one message group per user
options.rationale: FIFO keeps order, but a deleted message cannot be replayed, and each message goes to one consumer.

options.text: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
options.rationale: Records stay in order per partition key, many consumers can read the same stream, and records can be reread within the retention period.

questions.explanation: Choose a stream over a queue when several consumers need the same ordered records and replay.
